articles.summary: Fincantieri hosted Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao and senior federal officials at its Marinette and Sturgeon Bay shipyards in Wisconsin, highlighting investments in advanced manufacturing, automation and expanded shipbuilding capacity as the company prepares for construction of the U.S.
articles.body: U.S. Navy Secretary Visits Fincantieri Wisconsin Shipyards Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao visits Fincantieri shipyard in Wisconsin. Image courtesy Fincantieri Fincantieri hosted Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao and senior federal officials at its Marinette and Sturgeon Bay shipyards in Wisconsin, highlighting investments in advanced manufacturing, automation and expanded shipbuilding capacity as the company prepares for construction of the U.S. Navy's Landing Ship Medium (LSM) vessels . The delegation included Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, Maritime Administration Administrator Stephen Carmel, OMB Associate Director for Shipbuilding Jerry Hendrix and Eugenio Santagata , General Manager of Fincantieri's Naval Vessels Division. George Moutafis, CEO of Fincantieri Marine Group, and Jan Allman, CEO of Fincantieri Marinette Marine, outlined the company's shipbuilding programs, capital investments and efforts to accelerate production. At Marinette, officials toured the automated panel production line and observed demonstrations of collaborative robots, augmented and virtual reality tools, and powered air-purifying respirators. Fincantieri is integrating these technologies to improve production efficiency and worker safety. At Sturgeon Bay, the delegation reviewed the shipyard's capabilities and its role in supporting simultaneous construction of multiple vessel classes. "This vital federal investment allows us to modernize" is not part of this release; instead, Moutafis emphasized the company's investments in workforce capabilities and advanced technologies to increase production rates and meet Navy requirements. The visit comes as Fincantieri Marinette Marine prepares to begin construction of four LSM vessels for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, subject to negotiations with program manager TOTE Services. In April, the Navy awarded Fincantieri an initial $30 million contract for procurement of critical materials associated with the LSM program. "Our Navy needs more skilled professionals like those I had the opportunity to meet today in order to remain the strongest Navy in the world," Cao said. The Wisconsin facilities are positioned to serve as the industrial center for Fincantieri's LSM work, expanding their role in the U.S. naval shipbuilding industrial base. articles.summary: Sanmar Shipyards has delivered SAAM XIMBAL, a new BOGAÇAY Class tug, to SAAM Towage, marking the 18th SANMAR-built tug delivered to the towage operator since 2018.Known as BOGAÇAY XCVI during construction in Türkiye, SAAM XIMBAL will operate…
articles.body: 18th Tug Delivered by Sanmar Shipyards to SAAM Towage Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Sanmar Shipyards Sanmar Shipyards has delivered SAAM XIMBAL, a new BOGAÇAY Class tug, to SAAM Towage, marking the 18th SANMAR-built tug delivered to the towage operator since 2018. Known as BOGAÇAY XCVI during construction in Türkiye, SAAM XIMBAL will operate from the Port of Lázaro Cárdenas on Mexico's Pacific coast, supporting demanding ship-handling operations at one of the country's major commercial ports. SAAM XIMBAL is based on the RAmparts 2400SX-MK|I design, developed exclusively for SANMAR by Canadian naval architects Robert Allan Ltd. The latest delivery brings the number of BOGAÇAY Class tugs in the SAAM Towage fleet to 13. Powered by two CAT 3516E main engines, each producing 2,350 KW at 1,800 rpm, SAAM XIMBAL combines high performance with environmentally responsible operation. A high level of onboard automation supports operational efficiency, while a sewage treatment unit and oily water separator further reduce the vessel's environmental impact as per SAAM sustainability requisites With an overall length of 24.4 meters, a molded beam of 12 meters, a least moulded depth of 4.5 meters and a navigational draught of 5.45 meters, SAAM XIMBAL combines compact dimensions with the power required for demanding harbor operations. The tug delivers over 80 tonnes of bollard pull and achieves a free-running speed of 13 knots. It is also equipped with FiFi 1 firefighting capability, further enhancing its operational versatility. SAAM XIMBAL joins a diverse group of SANMAR-built vessels already operating in the SAAM Towage fleet. Alongside the 13 BOGAÇAY Class tugs, these include three all-electric ElectRA harbor tugs and two powerful BIGAÇAY Class RAstar 29005X tugs.

articles.title: Yinson Production, PTSC cheer FSO’s first oil at Southeast Asian project
articles.summary: Yinson Production and PTSC have achieved first oil ahead of schedule at a floating storage and offloading (FSO) vessel deployed offshore Vietnam.
articles.body: Exploration & Production October 23, 2026 · 3 hours ago Yinson Production, PTSC cheer FSO’s first oil at Southeast Asian project Yinson Production and PTSC have achieved first oil ahead of schedule at a floating storage and offloading (FSO) vessel deployed offshore Vietnam. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email FSO PTSC LDV moored offshore at Block 15-1 05 in Vietnam Source: Yinson Production Singapore’s Yinson Production, a subsidiary of Kuala Lumpur-based energy infrastructure and technology company Yinson, and PetroVietnam Technical Services Corporation (PTSC) have revealed a major operational milestone for a new dual-fuel floating storage and offloading unit, with first oil coming online at a field off the coast of Vietnam sooner than its expected fourth-quarter timeline. The FSO PTSC Lac Da Vang (FSO PTSC LDV) has reached its first oil operational milestone at the Lac Da Vang field in Block 15-1/05 offshore Vietnam on September 27, 2026, ahead of the previously communicated Q4 2026 schedule. The FSO features a storage capacity of 460,000 barrels and is designed to enhance operational efficiency while supporting sustainable offshore oilfield operations. Yinson Production emphasizes that this achievement represents a major milestone for the dual-fuel-powered newbuild FSO and the Lac Da Vang field, following provisional acceptance on September 20, 2026, which marked the start of the firm charter period. The FSO PTSC LDV is chartered to Murphy Cuu Long Bac Oil, a wholly owned subsidiary of Murphy Oil Corporation, under a ten-year firm contract with extension options of up to five additional years. The field's development is expected to ramp up through 2028 as additional wells are brought online, providing a vital new source of production to support Vietnam’s growing energy sector. Murphy Oil is the operator of Block 15-1/05 of the Cuu Long Basin with a 40% working interest, while its partners, PetroVietnam Exploration Production and SK Earthon, hold the remaining 35% and 25%, respectively. Flemming Guiducci Grønnegaard , Chief Executive Officer of Yinson Production, commented: "Achieving first oil for FSO PTSC LDV is a proud moment for Yinson Production and a major operational milestone for the Lac Da Vang field. “This achievement reflects the strong collaboration, technical excellence, and shared commitment to safety among Yinson Production, our joint venture partner PTSC, and our client, Murphy Oil Corporation. We look forward to delivering safe, reliable, and successful operations alongside our partners for years to come.” With a current fleet of 11 vessels, Yinson Production has an orderbook of approximately $19 billion until 2050 and global presence in 12 countries. articles.title: Mammoet, Port of Argentia Plan Floating Dry Dock, Marine Repair Facility
articles.summary: Mammoet Canada Eastern Ltd., Port of Argentia Inc. and Argentia Capital Inc. (ACI) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to advance plans for a floating dry dock and marine repair facility at the Port of Argentia in Newfoundland and Labrador…
articles.body: Mammoet, Port of Argentia Plan Floating Dry Dock, Marine Repair Facility Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Image courtesy Mammoet Image courtesy Mammoet Image courtesy Mammoet Image courtesy Mammoet Image courtesy Mammoet Mammoet Canada Eastern Ltd., Port of Argentia Inc. and Argentia Capital Inc. (ACI) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to advance plans for a floating dry dock and marine repair facility at the Port of Argentia in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada. The proposed development would combine Mammoet's heavy lifting, transport and marine engineering capabilities with the port's existing infrastructure, creating additional capacity for vessel maintenance, repair and industrial services. Central to the project is the Tugdock Submersible Platform (TSP) , developed by Mammoet subsidiary Tugdock Submersible Platforms Ltd. The modular floating dry dock system is designed to accommodate vessels of varying sizes and can be scaled to meet changing operational requirements, providing an alternative to conventional fixed dry dock infrastructure. The proposed facility would also leverage Argentia's existing graving dock, deepwater, ice-free harbor and extensive industrial property to support year-round operations. "This partnership represents an exciting opportunity to build on Mammoet's established presence at Argentia and introduce advanced, scalable marine technology to the Canadian market," said Jeremy Asher, Managing Director at Mammoet. The partners envision a multi-client facility serving commercial shipping, offshore oil and gas, offshore wind, the Canadian Coast Guard and the Royal Canadian Navy. Mammoet already operates at Argentia, including work associated with the former Cenovus Graving Dock site and offshore wind marshalling projects. Scott Penney, CEO of Port of Argentia, said the agreement builds on the port's existing relationship with Mammoet and opportunities emerging across Canada's marine industry. The partners will next initiate a formal Expression of Interest process to identify an experienced international marine industrial operator capable of managing the proposed facility. The MOU represents an initial development step, with the partners seeking to establish a competitive marine repair operation while expanding Newfoundland and Labrador's industrial capacity and creating opportunities for regional suppliers and skilled trades.

articles.title: NOIA Launches Ocean Minerals Initiative
articles.summary: The National Ocean Industries Association (NOIA) has launched Ocean Minerals Forward, a new industry education and communications initiative examining the potential of deep-sea mineral resources to strengthen U.S. critical mineral supply chains…
articles.body: NOIA Launches Ocean Minerals Initiative Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Courtesy NOIA The National Ocean Industries Association (NOIA) has launched Ocean Minerals Forward, a new industry education and communications initiative examining the potential of deep-sea mineral resources to strengthen U.S. critical mineral supply chains, support domestic manufacturing and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. The initiative includes a dedicated website, a comprehensive report and educational resources covering seabed mineral development, offshore technologies, environmental considerations and the regulatory challenges facing the emerging industry. Critical minerals including nickel, cobalt, copper, manganese and rare earth elements are increasingly important to defense systems, advanced manufacturing, energy infrastructure and digital technologies. With global processing and refining capacity concentrated in a limited number of countries, NOIA argues that ocean mineral resources could complement terrestrial mining, recycling and imports from allied nations. “America cannot afford to remain dependent on foreign-controlled supply chains for the minerals that power our economy and national defense,” said NOIA President Erik Milito. “The ocean holds significant mineral resources, and companies across the U.S. and allied nations are bringing the technology, offshore expertise, and investment needed to unlock their potential.” A central theme of the initiative is the potential application of existing offshore oil and gas industry capabilities to seabed mineral exploration and recovery. Click here to download the full report. NOIA points to decades of experience in deepwater operations, including subsea robotics, autonomous underwater vehicles, geophysical surveying, dynamic positioning, specialized offshore vessels and environmental monitoring. These technologies could provide a foundation for future ocean mineral projects while creating opportunities for U.S. shipyards, ports, subsea contractors and equipment manufacturers. Environmental considerations are also addressed, including the potential effects of sediment plumes, impacts on deep-sea biodiversity and the need for environmental assessments, monitoring and regulatory oversight. The Ocean Minerals Forward report examines resource potential, global supply chain concentration, China's role in mineral processing, emerging collection technologies and opportunities for American offshore companies. NOIA said it plans to expand the platform with additional research, industry case studies and updates as technology, regulation and commercial opportunities develop. The initiative comes as the offshore industry evaluates the technical, environmental and economic feasibility of commercial seabed mineral recovery, an emerging sector where significant questions remain about environmental impacts, permitting and the development of viable processing and supply chains.

articles.body: Romania Blames Russia for Ship Strike, Sinking Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 The Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Task Group (MCM TG) detects a drifting unmanned maritime system during a routine training exercise with our NATO partners and allies in the Black Sea, July 22, 2026. U.S. Navy photo by Lieutenant Tomas Jaramillo Romanian President Nicusor Dan accused Russia of escalating its attacks on NATO's eastern flank on Friday, after a drone strike sank a cargo ship off the Romanian Black Sea coast, killing at least one sailor with three still missing. Video released by Romanian authorities showed only a small part of the hull of the capsized tanker still visible above the waves as it sank. Emergency vessels were searching the surrounding waters for survivors in choppy seas and high wind. Romania's naval authority said the Comoros-flagged Khoryv, with a crew of 13 Ukrainian and Azeri sailors, had sent a distress signal 13 nautical miles off Romania's port of Constanta, just beyond Romanian territorial waters. Nine sailors were rescued from the water, three were missing and one body was recovered. The past two weeks have seen a sudden surge in deadly attacks on commercial ships off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, with at least seven cargo ships hit and some 30 sailors reported dead or missing. "It is part of Russia's escalation process in its war in Ukraine," President Dan told reporters, later saying the ship had been hit by a drone. NATO said on Tuesday it would send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea. The alliance has not specified what capabilities would be sent. On Saturday, Romanian jetsshot down two of the latest generation of Russian drones over Romanian territorial waters. The vessels that have been struck lately have either been anchored near or headed towards the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea. The canal has become the primary export route for Ukraine, one of the world's biggest grain and food oil exporters, which has relied on Danube River ports and Romanian territorial watersas Russia has attacked Ukraine's own Black Sea ports. Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria have called on NATO to do more to protect commercial shipping in the Black Sea. (Reuters)

articles.title: Port of Riga to test resilient maritime communications under new partnership
articles.summary: The Port of Riga will serve as a testing site for secure maritime communication technologies under a new partnership between LVR Flote and HARDMODE. The two companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) during the Techritory Forum in Riga on October 22, 2026. The agreement aims to develop and test...
articles.body: The Port of Riga will serve as a testing site for secure maritime communication technologies under a new partnership between LVR Flote and HARDMODE. The two companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) during the Techritory Forum in Riga on October 22, 2026. The agreement aims to develop and test communication systems that can support port operations during network disruptions and other challenging conditions. The partners will test new technologies in real port operations. They will also explore joint research projects and opportunities to introduce successful solutions at other European ports. Improving connectivity across port operations The project will focus on communication systems that remain operational when conventional networks become unavailable. HARDMODE develops solutions that combine several communication technologies. These include mobile, non-terrestrial, tactical and narrowband networks. The approach is designed to keep port equipment, sensors, vehicles, drones and personnel connected through different communication channels. It also uses a decentralized network structure, allowing connected devices to exchange information directly. Potential applications at the Port of Riga include infrastructure monitoring, hydrographic surveys, maintenance activities and navigation safety. The initiative comes amid concerns about GNSS interference in the Baltic Sea region, which has affected maritime activities in recent years. Partnership to support future port technologies LVR Flote provides technical services and supports infrastructure operations at the Port of Riga. Its involvement will allow the partners to assess new technologies against actual port requirements. “Port technical services have to keep running in everyday operations and in a crisis alike,” said Kaspars Ozoliņš, Member of the Board of LVR Flote. The companies also plan to create an open testing framework for other technology providers. This could include developers of monitoring systems, sensors, automation solutions and digital port services. HARDMODE will contribute its communication technology, while LVR Flote will provide operational expertise and access to real-world testing conditions. The partnership also creates opportunities for joint research between Latvia and the Netherlands, reflecting HARDMODE’s connections to both countries. The companies intend to explore how successful pilot projects could eventually be deployed across other European ports. However, the announcement does not specify an investment value or a timetable for the planned trials.

articles.summary: A little-known South Korean shipowner dominated oil transits through the Strait of Hormuz in September, data from intelligence firms suggest, with the group’s vessels moving more barrels than the next three owners combined.

Stock Photo: Nickeo23/Shutterstock By Weilun Soon Oct 23, 2026 (Bloomberg) –A little-known South Korean shipowner dominated oil transits through the Strait of Hormuz in September, data from intelligence firms suggest, with the group’s vessels moving more barrels than the next three owners combined. Ships owned by Sinokor Group carried 105.6 million barrels of crude through the waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with global markets, an analysis of ship-tracking and other data from intelligence firms Vortexa, Equasis and Signal Group showed. That’s equivalent to almost 40% of oil making the crossing last month. The next three players — the National Shipping Co. of Saudi Arabia, also known as Bahri, the Kuwait Oil Tanker Company, and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co.’s shipping unit — accounted for a combined 97.3 million barrels during the same period, according to Bloomberg calculations based on that data. The analysis considered ownership and not vessel operators. None of the four companies replied to requests for comment. Sinokor, owned by tycoon Ga-Hyun Chung, gained prominence from the early weeks of the Iran war, having amassed a huge tanker fleet in the run up to the conflict through purchases or time charters. When Hormuz was all but closed off, those tankers were snapped up at exorbitant rates by producers who needed to load oil or risk running out of storage space and then being forced to undertake costly shutdowns. Read more: Iran War Supercharges Secretive Korean Tycoon’s Big Tanker Bet As Gulf crude exports recover to close to pre-war levels, Sinokor is still among the most active owners in the so-called shuttling trade, with its vessels taking short trips to pick up oil from inside the Persian Gulf, sail through Hormuz and then discharge at ship-to-ship transfer points in the Gulf of Oman. Its tankers have assisted in the transporting of crude from Saudi Arabia and the UAE, and more recently also dabbled in Iraq and Qatar shipments, ship-tracking data show. October 23, 2026 (Credit: Kiewit) HD Hyundai and Kiewit Maritime Co. have announced plans to establish a joint venture to develop a new shipyard in the United States, targeting the start of construction in 2027 and full-scale operations in 2029. The proposed venture, HD Kiewit Shipbuilding LLC, would combine HD Hyundai's shipbuilding technology and shipyard operating expertise with Kiewit's engineering, construction and fabrication capabilities, the companies said. The shipyard is planned for an existing industrial site with deep water and unrestricted access to the Gulf, with the facility potentially supporting up to 3,000 jobs at full operating capacity. The venture will initially explore opportunities in naval auxiliary and commercial vessel construction, as well as ship block and module fabrication for U.S. shipbuilders. The companies also plan to explore cooperation in maritime infrastructure and support the development of domestic supply chains for marine components and logistics. The proposed facility would incorporate HD Hyundai's Future of Shipyard (FOS) model, including digital twins, automated production systems and robotic welding, aimed at improving shipbuilding productivity, quality and safety. Kiewit Maritime, an affiliate of Kiewit Offshore Services, would contribute large-scale fabrication and construction capabilities, supported by its affiliate's facilities and experience. The companies also intend to support technical training and workforce development as part of the proposed shipyard project.

articles.summary: Freight, not relative diesel prices, has closed the US arbitrage into Europe. Rates for prompt US Gulf Coast cargoes have climbed from around 250 to over 400 worldscale, closing the arbs, before settling lower in recent sessions to come closer to an equilibrium. articles.body: Diesel arbitrage: why freight has shut the Europe import window in International Shipping News 23/10/2026 Freight, not relative diesel prices, has closed the US arbitrage into Europe. Rates for prompt US Gulf Coast cargoes have climbed from around 250 to over 400 worldscale, closing the arbs, before settling lower in recent sessions to come closer to an equilibrium. That does not mean supply stops. Supply is being pulled by relative economics, and we need to look at both sides of the import/export coin to determine where flows will move. What is the diesel arbitrage, and why is it red? The diesel arbitrage is the difference between the delivered cost of a diesel cargo from an origin port and the price a buyer will pay at the destination. When the sale price is below the landed cost, the arbitrage is closed, and a third party cannot buy, ship and sell the cargo at a profit. For November arrivals in Rotterdam, every origin on the board is currently negative. The gap ranges from small (US Gulf Coast, around $1/bbl closed) to wide (West Coast India, roughly $60-70/t closed) or even ultra-wide (Ulsan, around $150/t closed). Diesel is a near-global commodity, so the comparison is origin port against origin port rather than grade against grade. Market context: a long conflict and a lopsided barrel Almost eight months into the Middle East conflict, headline crude flows have recovered. The seven-day average is around 24 million b/d, against a pre-war baseline of 23 million b/d. Products have not followed. Exports from the Gulf are still about 50% below pre-war levels, and waterways remain contested, with 18 vessels attacked in an 11-day window. Prices reflect the imbalance. Brent for December trades just under $110/bbl, while November ICE gasoil is around $1,477/t, close to $200/bbl. Diesel is propping up the complex, while the rest of the barrel drags it down. Key insights Freight closed the window the market opened From about 20 September to early October, buyers could pay almost any freight rate for US Gulf Coast diesel into Europe and still profit. That demand pushed rates from a typical 250 worldscale to over 400. The arbitrage closed because costs rose faster than the sales price, and indeed that sales price came off as news (Russian sanctions relief, SPR releases) eased supply crunch expectations in Europe. The sensitivity is precise. Lower the freight input to 330 worldscale and the Houston to Rotterdam arbitrage just about opens. For freight traders, that gives a reference level: • TC14 was near 400 worldscale at the end of last week. • Tonnage supply is rising: about 180 vessels are signalling ballast within 15 days of the Gulf Coast, a sign that capacity is building. • Reopening level: with other inputs unchanged, a TC14 move towards 340-350 worldscale reopens the arbitrage, which makes it a possible target for a short position. Physical differentials can swing the arbitrage faster than paper The sales price used in the arbitrage is a premium to the swap, set by physical buyers. It moved from +$25/t on 12 October to -$4/t on 19 October, a $30/t swing in a week on late-Nov arrivals. The move came as the market weighed possible strategic reserve releases and diplomatic efforts to secure more Middle East diesel for Europe. Only broker-sourced physical differentials show this kind of shift. Red arbitrages do not stop diesel moving Refiners keep running because they earn the crack, and the diesel has to go somewhere. West Coast India into Rotterdam is closed by $60-70/t, but it is less closed than India into Singapore, so those barrels still point west. The flow data supports the point: • India to Europe diesel flows were suppressed from March to June, when the economics pointed east. • Flows returned from July. September was one of the highest months in a long time, after the arbitrage opened for third parties in August. • Short-haul Yanbu to Mediterranean runs remain open. Origin-owned barrels behave differently from third-party barrels. An owner of the molecule moves it west at a profit even when a third party cannot. Arbitrage signals lead flows, with a lag Open windows show up in fixtures first. October-loading fixtures jumped from 336 kt to over 1 million tonnes within a few days, coinciding with the open arbitrage in late September and early October. In the spring, an arbitrage signal in late March and early April translated into a rise in flows by May. Comparing a five-day arbitrage signal with a 28-day flow average therefore means allowing for roughly a month. The supply picture is a Russia and US story, not only a Middle East story The US Gulf Coast supplied almost half of North West Europe’s diesel imports over the past 12 months, a much larger share than a year earlier. US refiners have run hard since April and filled a gap left by missing Russian barrels in markets such as Brazil and the Americas. Any US diesel export restriction would therefore hit both the Middle East shortfall and the Russian one. Meanwhile the Jizan refinery on the Red Sea is not expected back until the end of December. Implications for traders and decision-makers • Timing matters. A first-window January discharge into Europe needs Houston loading around mid-December. Via the Cape from Jamnagar, loading is needed around 25 November. Decisions are due weeks before the arrival month. • European demand is soft. Refiners have shifted yields towards distillates and demand has been weak, so Europe’s North West net balance sits above its seasonal range. Warmer winter expectations help. Stocks, however, have been drawn down and will need rebuilding. • Arbitrages open briefly. Historically, a Gulf Coast window opens for a day or two, long enough to fix a batch of vessels, and then closes until the market needs to pull barrels again. • Non-economic flows exist. Government-to-government deals and policy moves do not follow arbitrage economics, so treat the signal as a guide to marginal barrels, not total flows. For new routes without published prices, such as Russian diesel into the US, use proxies and override the inputs: a worldscale assumption for freight and an assumed differential for the cargo. At one illustrative set of inputs, landing in New York would still be 24 cents/gal below the sales price. Key takeaways • Freight is the swing variable: around 330 worldscale reopens the US Gulf Coast to Rotterdam arbitrage. • A $30/t move in physical differentials in one week shows why broker-sourced cash data matters. • Closed arbitrages still carry flows; watch relative economics, not only the sign. Conclusion For November and December arrivals, Europe is not in dire straits, but the supply chain depends on a narrow set of marginal sources: Gulf Coast barrels when freight dips, and Indian and Saudi cargoes when east-west economics favour Europe. The next test is freight. If TC14 and prompt rates fall towards the 330-350 worldscale area while tonnage supply builds, expect the Gulf Coast window to reopen and fixtures to follow within days. If not, Europe’s resupply leans on the barrels that already point west. Test these views yourself. articles.body: eBL adoption passes halfway mark in International Shipping News 23/10/2026 Electronic bill of lading (eBL) adoption has reached 51.1%, according to the FIT Alliance’s 2026 global survey, up from 49.2% in 2024 and 33% in 2022. BIMCO is a founding member of the alliance. The findings indicate that eBL use is becoming more established: 11.2% of respondents now use eBLs exclusively, compared with 7.5% in 2024. As adoption grows, the industry’s focus is shifting from legal acceptance towards practical implementation. Interoperability and platform fragmentation were the concerns cited most frequently by respondents, followed by legal effectiveness and authenticity verification, and implementation and onboarding at scale. The survey confirms that interoperability is now a central concern for scaling eBL adoption. The industry has made important progress, but the next phase must enable electronic trade documents and trusted data to move securely and efficiently across different platforms, jurisdictions and participants. Strong support for digital transformation The business case for eBLs remains widely recognised. Some 93.8% of respondents regard them as an enabler of broader digital transformation in trade, broadly unchanged from 94% in 2024. Faster processing was ranked as the leading benefit, followed by improved handling, greater data accuracy, enhanced security and cost savings. Around two-thirds of respondents also considered reduced paper use and lower transport emissions important. Banking adoption remains limited Banks continue to lag behind the wider market. Just 22.2% of bank respondents reported at least partial eBL use, compared with 21.1% in 2024. According to the survey, wider banking adoption will require assurance that the control, status and transfer of an eBL can be verified as it moves between platforms and participants—not only within an individual provider’s system. The FIT Alliance argues that eBLs must ultimately become portable, structured and standards-based data objects capable of moving across systems and jurisdictions. The FIT Alliance and its partners are committed to advancing this collective effort and turning interoperability into a practical reality for global trade. articles.body: ZEMBA concludes inaugural tender with Hapag-Lloyd in International Shipping News 23/10/2026 The Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance (ZEMBA) has delivered 82,000 mtCO2-equivalent (mtCO2e) in emissions reductions in 2025 and 2026 under its first low-emission shipping tender with Hapag-Lloyd, which concluded this month. The reductions were achieved through the use of liquefied biomethane (LBM) across eight international shipping voyages under 17 contracts between Hapag-Lloyd and ZEMBA members. The German container liner secured ZEMBA’s inaugural tender to replace conventional bunker fuels with lower-emission alternatives. Under the arrangement, Hapag-Lloyd used waste-based LBM on some of the dual-fuel vessels in its LNG-capable fleet to reduce well-to-wake greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. It then allocated environmental attribute certificates representing the emissions reductions achieved during these voyages to ZEMBA members through a book-and-claim mechanism. The mechanism allowed cargo owners to claim emissions reductions by paying a premium for lower-emission shipping services, even if their cargo was transported on vessels running on conventional marine fuels. ZEMBA members include major cargo owners such as Amazon, Nike, IKEA and Patagonia. Second tender moves to e-fuels ZEMBA has awarded its second tender to Hapag-Lloyd and Norwegian shipping company North Sea Container Line (NCL), with fuel deliveries scheduled to begin in 2027. Hapag-Lloyd will use e-methanol on a trans-oceanic trade route, while NCL will deploy green ammonia on a northern European route. Both fuels will be produced using green hydrogen generated with renewable energy and are expected to deliver lifecycle emissions reductions of at least 90% compared with conventional marine fuels. ZEMBA expects the two companies to collectively deliver around 120,000 mtCO2e in emissions reductions over three years from 2027. Its members will again pay a premium for the associated reductions through a book-and-claim mechanism. articles.summary: Around 6,000 seafarers remain trapped near the Strait of Hormuz, as attacks on commercial vessels intensify and concerns grow over the safety of crews caught in the continuing conflict between the US and Iran, according to the head of the UN’s maritime agency. articles.body: 6,000 seafarers trapped as attacks deepen Strait of Hormuz shipping crisis in International Shipping News 23/10/2026 Around 6,000 seafarers remain trapped near the Strait of Hormuz, as attacks on commercial vessels intensify and concerns grow over the safety of crews caught in the continuing conflict between the US and Iran, according to the head of the UN’s maritime agency. International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez warned on Sunday that conditions had become increasingly dangerous, with reports of 24 ships attacked in roughly two weeks and no guarantees of safe passage through one of the world’s most important shipping routes. “The situation continues to be severe and critical when it comes to international shipping,” Dominguez told Fox News Digital, explaining that “there is a double blockade and too many vessels have been attacked, particularly in recent days.” The consequences for those working at sea have been particularly serious. According to the IMO, 100 maritime incidents had been confirmed across the region as of October 9, while 24 seafarers have lost their lives since the conflict began on February 28. With thousands of crew members still unable to leave the area safely, Dominguez urged vessels to avoid transiting the Strait until adequate assurances could be provided. “Seafarers have continued to perish in these attacks and around 6,000 seafarers remain trapped since the beginning of the conflict,” he said, making clear that his message was not to transit the waterway or put crews at further risk “until we have guarantees.” However, attacks on vessels are not the only concern. A separate dispute has emerged over the alleged misuse of VHF Channel 16, the internationally designated maritime distress and safety frequency, following accusations by Tehran that American military forces have been using it to threaten Iranian civilian crews. In a letter circulated to IMO member states on October 9, Iran claimed that “VHF Channel 16 has been repeatedly occupied for prolonged periods by the United States military forces operating in the Persian Gulf.” The letter went further, alleging that “during such transmissions, Iranian seafarers have been addressed in Persian with threatening, abusive and provocative language and in certain instances urged to abandon their vessels.” Tehran accused Washington of turning a channel intended for maritime safety into an “instrument of military intimidation and psychological pressure against civilian crews”, and called on the IMO to raise the matter with member states and relevant international organisations. Nevertheless, the accusations remain unverified. Although Iran referred to information from commercial vessels, shipping companies and maritime operators, it provided no recordings, transcripts or specific examples of the alleged communications. For its part, US Central Command (CENTCOM) defended its enforcement of the naval blockade of Iranian ports, maintaining that shipping operators were properly informed and given sufficient opportunities to comply. “The US naval blockade has been in place for months and is professionally communicated to all international mariners,” CENTCOM said, adding that “vessels that refuse to comply with blockade enforcement receive multiple warnings, with ample opportunity to comply.” The disagreement has raised wider questions about the protection of maritime communication channels during military confrontations, particularly when civilian vessels find themselves operating in increasingly dangerous waters. Dominguez stressed that merchant seafarers should not be treated as participants in military conflicts, pointing out that “seafarers are not trained for combat, and they are not guilty of any conflicts that are happening around the world.” He also expressed concern that Channel 16, whose primary purpose is to facilitate distress and safety communications, could be used for messages that crews might reasonably interpret as threatening. While the IMO has not announced a formal investigation, its secretary-general said the organisation could examine whether its existing procedures and regulatory framework needed strengthening to prevent similar incidents. At the same time, another problem is complicating an already dangerous situation. According to Dominguez, fraudulent ship registrations and vessels operating under false flags have become increasingly prominent, with some operators continuing to transport cargo through the region despite the risks involved. He warned that such practices were contributing to the escalation, particularly where ships were being used to move goods in and out of the affected area without adequate regard for crew safety. Despite the continuing confrontation, diplomatic communication between the IMO and Iran has not broken down. Dominguez confirmed that he remains in contact with Iranian representatives through official channels, although he has no direct communication with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. “I have conversations with them and they respond to my messages. You know, the information flows,” he explained, before acknowledging that “what is difficult is to get final decisions because of the conflict that is ongoing.” Source: Cyprus Mail 2026-10-23 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: China and Djibouti stress need to protect Red Sea shipping lanes in International Shipping News 23/10/2026 All countries should enjoy freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, China and Djibouti said in a joint statement following a meeting of their foreign ministers in Beijing, expressing concern about the deteriorating security situation. Djibouti sits on the other side of the Bab al-Mandab Strait from Yemen, where Iran-backed Houthis have been battling Saudi-backed government forces and seeking to control the whole Yemeni Red Sea coast, disrupting some shipping. In 2017, China formally opened its first overseas military base in Djibouti. The barren former French colony, which is about the size of Wales, is sandwiched between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Somalia and also hosts US, Japanese and French bases. The joint statement, released early on Thursday, said both China and Djibouti stressed the importance of maintaining freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and the strait, and “emphasised the right of merchant ships of all countries to exercise navigation rights in accordance with international law should be respected”. “Both sides believe that in governing and securing the Red Sea, the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and wishes of the Red Sea littoral states should be genuinely respected, avoiding any increase in the overall security risks of the region.” China supports the littoral states of the Red Sea in “constructively maintaining” the safety and smooth flow of international shipping lanes, said the statement, carried by China’s official Xinhua news agency. Neither country wants regional tensions to spill further into the Red Sea, and “major powers outside the region” should respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of regional countries, and avoid resorting to force and unilateral sanctions, it added. The statement came as the US State Department ordered some diplomats and family members to depart from its missions in Saudi Arabia following the escalation of the fighting in Yemen, which has opened another front in the regional conflict triggered by the US-Israeli war on Iran. articles.title: India introduces new requirements for ships in coastal waters
articles.summary: Expanded scope of the 2026 Rules India notified the Merchant Shipping (Regulation of Entry of Ships into Coastal Waters) Rules, 2026 on 16 September 2026. The Rules supersede the Merchant Shipping (Regulation of Entry of Ships into Ports, Anchorages and Offshore Facilities) Rules, 2012. The new regime applies to...
articles.body: India introduces new requirements for ships in coastal waters in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 23/10/2026 Expanded scope of the 2026 Rules India notified the Merchant Shipping (Regulation of Entry of Ships into Coastal Waters) Rules, 2026 on 16 September 2026. The Rules supersede the Merchant Shipping (Regulation of Entry of Ships into Ports, Anchorages and Offshore Facilities) Rules, 2012. The new regime applies to Indian ships and to foreign ships that operate in or navigate through Indian coastal waters, whether or not they enter an Indian port, anchorage or offshore facility. The absence of an Indian port call therefore does not necessarily place a foreign ship outside the scope of the Rules. What is meant by “coastal waters”? The 2026 Rules refer to the definition in the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. Under section 3(12): • “Coastal waters” means any part of territorial waters of India, along with any part of the adjoining maritime zones of India within the meaning of the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976 (80 of 1976), or any other law for time being in force; • It covers India’s territorial sea and adjoining maritime zones, including areas beyond the territorial sea where India has rights or jurisdiction under the relevant laws. Key requirements Insurance and financial security Foreign ships within the scope of the Rules must maintain the applicable insurance or other financial security required under the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 and the relevant rules. For ships calling at an Indian port, the port authority may verify the validity of the cover. Evidence of class A foreign ship exceeding the applicable age threshold must hold a valid certificate of class issued by an International Association of Classification Societies (IACS) member or a recognised organisation. The thresholds highlighted in the available industry guidance are: • Oil product and chemical tankers: over 10 years. • LNG and LPG tankers: over 15 years. • General cargo ships, bulk carriers, offshore support ships, passenger ships and other specified ship types: generally over 10 years. Salvage and marine pollution response contracts Foreign ships entering, remaining in or sailing from an Indian port, seeking port facilities, or transiting or operating within Indian coastal waters are required to maintain valid salvage and marine pollution response contracts with an entity approved under the applicable Indian legislation. The purpose is to ensure that response support is available in the event of a casualty, pollution incident or other emergency. Port calls and transits: an important distinction The new Rules apply not only to ships calling at Indian ports, anchorages or offshore facilities, but also to ships operating in or navigating through Indian coastal waters. As a result, a foreign ship may still fall within the scope of the Rules even if it is only transiting Indian coastal waters and has no intention of calling at an Indian port. For ships calling at an Indian port, the requirements may include applicable insurance or financial security, evidence of class, and salvage and marine pollution response arrangements. These ships must also comply with the port-entry documentation requirements, including submission of the prescribed documents at least 48 hours before entering the port. Ships that are only transiting or operating in Indian coastal waters may still be subject to the requirements relating to insurance or financial security, class, and salvage and marine pollution response arrangements. However, the 48-hour documentation requirement may not apply to such vessels. Transition period until April 2027 The Directorate General of Maritime Administration issued Circular No. 69 of 2026 on 14 October 2026. The Circular explains that the process of approving salvors and marine pollution response operators is still underway and that the relevant contract requirement cannot be fully implemented until approved providers have been notified. To allow an orderly transition, ships already operating in, or otherwise permitted entry into, Indian coastal waters have been given six months, up to April 2027, to comply with the additional requirements introduced by the 2026 Rules. By that date, owners and operators are expected to comply with the revised classification requirements and maintain the required salvage and marine pollution response contracts. Further guidance expected At the time of writing, the empanelment of approved salvors and marine pollution response operators remains in progress. Further clarification is also expected on contracting arrangements. Owners and operators should continue to monitor official DGMA updates and obtain voyage-specific advice from their local agents where necessary. articles.body: HD Hyundai Launches Largest Ammonia Vessel in Shipbuilding News 23/10/2026 The world’s largest ammonia-powered vessel, measuring 230 meters in length and 36.5 meters in width, has made its debut in Ulsan. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries held a naming ceremony for the 93,000-cubic-meter very large ammonia-powered carrier Terra Clove at its Ulsan shipyard on Oct. 22. The vessel is the first of two sister ships that HD Hyundai Heavy Industries won in an order from Singapore-based EPS in 2023. The name Terra Clove combines “Terra,” the Latin word for earth, and “Clove,” meaning flower bud, reflecting environmentally friendly values. About 110 officials attended the event to celebrate the launch of the new vessel, including Lee Sang-kyun, Vice Chairman and Head of HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, EPS CEO Cyril Ducau, and Loh Koon Yen, chairman of the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore. At the core of Terra Clove is its ammonia dual-fuel propulsion system. The vessel was designed to selectively use conventional marine fuel oil and ammonia, an eco-friendly fuel, depending on operating conditions. In particular, it incorporates advanced disaster-prevention technologies, including a real-time ammonia leak detection device and an emission reduction system, securing safety, the biggest challenge for ammonia-powered ships. Its transport capacity and efficiency have also been maximized. Equipped with four cargo tanks designed and built in-house by HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, the vessel can stably transport both ammonia and liquefied petroleum gas, or LPG, at the same time. It is also fitted with a shaft generator that produces electricity using the propulsion engine’s rotating shaft, as well as nitrogen oxides and sulfur oxides reduction systems, strengthening its ability to meet environmental regulations. Through the construction of this vessel, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries once again demonstrated its technological edge in the ammonia-powered ship sector. In April, it delivered the world’s first 46,000-cubic-meter medium-sized ammonia-powered gas carrier. At the naming ceremony, Lee Sang-kyun, Vice Chairman and Head of HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, said, “It is an honor to have built next-generation eco-friendly ships together with EPS,” adding, “The construction of this world’s largest ammonia-powered vessel is an important step forward toward the decarbonization of shipping.” After final outfitting work, Terra Clove is scheduled to be delivered to shipowner EPS in early November. articles.body: MPA and Eastern Pacific Shipping Mark Christening of Singapore-Registered Ammonia Dual-Fuelled Vessel in Port News 23/10/2026 The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) and Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) marked the christening of Terra Clove at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HHI) in Ulsan, South Korea. The 93,000-cubic-metre Very Large Ammonia Carrier (VLAC) is EPS’ first ammonia dual-fuelled vessel and the first ammonia dual-fuelled commercial newbuild vessel to be registered under the Singapore Registry of Ships (SRS). It is equipped with Everllence’s first commercial ammonia dual-fuelled two-stroke marine engine, which successfully completed factory acceptance testing in April 2026. The vessel is the result of a collaboration initiated in June 2022 by MPA, EPS, HHI, and the American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) to develop an ammonia dual-fuelled gas carrier under the Singapore flag. Terra Clove is the first of two such vessels being built by HHI for EPS, both of which will be registered under the Singapore flag. Designed to transport ammonia as cargo and use it as propulsion fuel, Terra Clove incorporates specialised ammonia fuel handling, containment, and safety systems. The vessel is expected to be delivered in November 2026, following its upcoming sea trials. As Singapore’s flag administration, MPA has worked closely with EPS, HHI, ABS, and other industry partners on the vessel’s technical and regulatory compliance. This included reviewing the vessel’s design against relevant International Maritime Organization (IMO) guidelines, participating in hazard identification and operability studies, and providing regulatory guidance on ammonia detection, fuel system safety, and emissions management. MPA also shared its experience from earlier ammonia trials to support the development of onboard safety procedures and crew preparedness. Mr Ang Wee Keong, Chief Executive of MPA, said, “Developing new technologies often comes with some uncertainties. Terra Clove shows that by bringing together expertise from across the maritime value chain, we can help address these uncertainties and investment risks, and give partners the confidence to move forward together. We hope the successful development of this vessel will give the wider industry greater confidence in ammonia as a marine fuel.” Mr Cyril Ducau, Chief Executive Officer of EPS, said, “The naming of Terra Clove marks an important milestone towards making ammonia a viable marine fuel. Beyond developing the technology, our priority is ensuring its safe and practical operation. With MPA’s regulatory guidance and the support of HHI, ABS, Everllence, and our other partners, we are building the expertise and capabilities needed to advance the safe adoption of ammonia as a marine fuel.” Source: Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore 2026-10-23 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: A fund managed by IFM Investors has agreed to acquire a 63.9% stake in Associated British Ports (ABP), one of the United Kingdom’s largest port operators. The agreement involves the acquisition of the entire shareholdings held by Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPP Investments) and OMERS. CPP Investments will sell its 33.9% interest, while OMERS will divest its 30% stake. The transaction will give the IFM-managed fund majority ownership of ABP, subject to the required approvals. Major investment in UK port infrastructure Associated British Ports plays a significant role in the UK’s maritime and logistics sectors. Its network handles approximately a quarter of the country’s seaborne trade. The company operates major port facilities, including Southampton, Immingham and Hull. These ports support container shipping, automotive logistics, bulk cargo and other commercial activities. The proposed acquisition represents a significant ownership change for a major UK port infrastructure business. It also highlights the continued involvement of institutional investors in maritime infrastructure. Transaction expected to close in 2027 The agreement will see CPP Investments and OMERS exit their existing investments in ABP. The transaction remains subject to customary closing conditions, including the necessary regulatory approvals. Until these requirements are satisfied, the existing ownership arrangements remain in place. The companies expect the transaction to be completed in the first half of 2027. The announcement confirms the agreed transfer of the majority stake but does not disclose the purchase price. Following completion, the IFM-managed fund will hold a controlling interest in one of the UK’s most important port infrastructure operators.

articles.title: Rio Tinto targets larger capesizes in $1.9bn Australian bauxite push
articles.summary: Mining giant Rio Tinto has approved a $1.9bn investment in a major bauxite expansion in Australia’s Queensland state, including an upgrade of its export facilities to accommodate larger capesize bulk carriers. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Operations Rio Tinto targets larger capesizes in $1.9bn Australian bauxite push Adis Ajdin October 23, 2026 0 38 2 minutes read Bocimar Bocimar Mining giant Rio Tinto has approved a $1.9bn investment in a major bauxite expansion in Australia’s Queensland state, including an upgrade of its export facilities to accommodate larger capesize bulk carriers. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production capacity, with first output targeted for 2029 and full production expected by 2032. The development will replace production from the ageing Andoom mine near Weipa, which is expected to reach the end of its life this decade, while also helping offset the planned closure of the Gove operation in the Northern Territory in 2029. Once fully operational, Kangwinan will lift annual capacity at Rio Tinto’s Weipa operations to around 44m tonnes, compared with current production of approximately 38m tonnes. The new mining centre will be located about 15 km southeast of Rio Tinto’s existing Amrun mine. A 15 km conveyor system will transport bauxite to expanded stockyards and the Amrun export wharf, which will be upgraded to handle larger capesize vessels. The mining group said the port expansion would improve shipping efficiency and reduce freight costs, strengthening its ability to supply overseas customers and Australian alumina refineries. Despite the larger vessels and additional mining capacity, analysts at SEB see limited upside for the capesize market from the investment. The bank noted that much of the new production will replace output from existing mines, leaving a relatively modest increase of around 6m tonnes compared with current Weipa production levels. Any additional volumes are also several years away. SEB further pointed out that shipments from Australia to China involve voyages roughly 3.3 times shorter than those from Guinea, where surging bauxite exports have been a major driver of capesize tonne-mile demand. The bank argued that additional Australian volumes could therefore work against the shift towards longer-haul Guinea-China trades, with the overall impact on dry bulk shipping likely to be negligible. Construction at Kangwinan is scheduled to accelerate in 2027, with the investment including $150m already approved for early works last year. The latest commitment follows Rio Tinto’s September agreement to acquire the neighbouring Aurukun bauxite project from Glencore and Mitsubishi, subject to regulatory approvals. The company intends to integrate the deposit into its longer-term development plans for the region, using existing and planned infrastructure. Bauxite’s growing importance to dry bulk shipping will be reflected at next April’s Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, with a standalone Bauxite Blitz session. Scheduled for April 28, the discussion will examine the expanding trade, shifting supply patterns and implications for future capesize demand. Confirmed speakers include Ernst Meyer, president and CEO of Torvald Klaveness, and Robert Haggquist, charterer and decarbonisation lead at South32. Braemar’s Derek Langston will moderate the session. The project represents an investment of approximately INR 22.76 billion. Once completed, the terminal will have an annual cargo-handling capacity of 18.33 million tonnes. The development will take place under a public-private partnership (PPP) model, with Essar Ports and the port authority contributing to the investment. The concession agreement will cover a period of 30 years. The new facilities will expand cargo-handling capacity at Kandla, one of India’s major ports on the country’s western coast. The project will also support the port’s ability to handle larger vessels and a wider range of cargo operations. The planned terminal will add new capacity for multipurpose cargo handling. It will also strengthen the port infrastructure available to businesses moving goods through the region. The investment forms part of efforts to improve port facilities and support maritime trade in India. However, the Letter of Award represents a project development milestone rather than the start of commercial operations. The announcement does not provide a confirmed construction timetable or opening date for the new terminal.

articles.title: Eni, PTTEP forge JV to consolidate stakes in ADNOC’s giant offshore sour gas asset
articles.summary: PTTEP and Eni have created Seela Energies to streamline operations and combine their stakes in an ADNOC-operated concession off the coast of the UAE.
articles.body: Business & Finance October 23, 2026 · 7 hours ago Eni, PTTEP forge JV to consolidate stakes in ADNOC’s giant offshore sour gas asset PTTEP and Eni have created Seela Energies to streamline operations and combine their stakes in an ADNOC-operated concession off the coast of the UAE. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Hail and Ghasha island under construction Source ADNOC As one of the world’s largest sour gas mega-projects continues to take shape in the waters of the Arabian Gulf, two energy heavyweights, Thailand’s PTT Exploration and Production Public Company (PTTEP) and Italy’s Eni, have pooled their stakes in Abu Dhabi’s massive Ghasha concession, carving out a newly minted joint venture (JV) called Seela Energies to unlock financing, share deep technical expertise, and scale up their activities for the long haul. PTTEP MENA, PTTEP’s wholly owned subsidiary, together with Eni Abu Dhabi, has established Seela Energies, with each company holding a 50% shareholding. Each of the founders holds a 10% participating interest in the Ghasha concession project , which will now be transferred to the newly formed JV. As a result, the duo will hold an indirect 10% interest in the project. According to PTTEP, all required regulatory, governmental, and partner approvals have been obtained, and all conditions precedent have been fulfilled. “The establishment of Seela Energies strengthens the collaboration between PTTEP and Eni, enhances access to financing, builds capability, shares expertise and supports potential future mutual growth in Middle East region, in line with PTTEP’s strategy to deliver long-term value through strategic partnerships,” emphasized the Thai player. Related Articles Fossil Energy WATCH: First steel cut for mega gas project set on zero-emission ops by entwining smart tech, carbon capture, hydrogen, nuclear, and renewable power 7 min read The Ghasha concession offshore Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates, which is operated by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), is expected to produce more than 1.8 billion standard cubic feet of gas per day and 150,000 barrels of oil and condensate per day over the long term. This concession is considered to be one of the world's largest sulfur-rich gas development projects and a cornerstone of the UAE's strategy to achieve gas self-sufficiency and support rising international export demand. The development concept encompasses multiple fields, including Hail and Ghasha , located in shallow waters. This project utilizes a series of artificial islands rather than traditional platforms to drill and manage operations while minimizing environmental disturbance. Related Articles Fossil Energy First jacket comes to slide into place at huge offshore gas project 3 min read The Hail and Ghasha project, designed with an emphasis on low-emissions technology, aims to operate with net-zero carbon emissions by integrating carbon capture with a target of around 1.5 million tonnes of CO2 per year, low-carbon hydrogen use to replace fuel gas, and relying on less-emission-intensive power sources, such as nuclear and solar. ADNOC’s partners in the Ghasha concession, aside from Eni and PTTEP, which consolidated their joint stakes under Seela Energies, involved other companies across the broader project lifecycle, including Wintershall Dea, OMV, and Lukoil. The Ghasha development is envisioned to employ smart technology across all operations, allowing operators, technicians, and site personnel remote access to the project’s operations. Aside from a fully unmanned facility, ADNOC has set its sights on artificial intelligence (AI), such as predictive maintenance, for all critical rotating equipment. A few months ago, the operator, in partnership with Eni and PTTEP, put into place a structured financing transaction of up to $11 billion (AED 40.4 billion) for Hail and Ghasha sour gas development. The UAE giant’s financing model follows a series of midstream and infrastructure transactions, including a $4.9 billion (AED 18 billion) oil pipeline partnership and a $10.1 billion (AED 37.1 billion) gas pipeline agreement. It also comes after build-own-operate-transfer (BOOT) projects, such as the $3.8 billion (AED 14 billion) project to power and decarbonize offshore operations and the $2.2 billion (AED 8.3 billion) project to deliver sustainable water supplies to onshore operations. articles.title: Tanker Oil Spill Forces Closure of Beaches in UAE
articles.summary: An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the coast of Umm Al Quwain, prompting containment operations and environmental assessments, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday.The ministry said all…
articles.body: Tanker Oil Spill Forces Closure of Beaches in UAE Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Алексей Закиров / Adobe Stock The United Arab Emirates said efforts were under way on Friday to contain oil leaking from a tanker vessel offshore that prompted authorities to close beaches and warn fishermen to avoid the area. Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout. The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said in a statement that containment operations had been launched and an environmental assessment was being carried out. All beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain had been temporarily closed until technical teams completed their assessments and determined the necessary safety and marine protection measures, it said. The ministry also urged fishermen and other sea users to avoid affected areas and follow official instructions. Authorities in Sharjah temporarily closed Al Hamriyah Beach, on the UAE's northern coast near the border with Umm Al Quwain, as a precaution, the Sharjah Government Media Bureau said. ANALYST IDENTIFIES LEAKING TANKER AS THE GEM NO.2 UAE authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. The environment ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, told Reuters that the spill was coming from a tanker called the Gem No.2 and analysts say satellite imagery from October 19 and 21 appears to show a significant oil slick from the tanker. "The slick is considerably larger, covering approximately 160 km2, and looks to be coming from the ship," Leon Moreland, researcher at the Conflict and Environment Observatory, said. "Furthermore, a slick this close to shore increases the chance it could impact nearby beaches and ecologically sensitive habitats," he said. Shipping sources said on October 9 that the Gem No.2 was struck by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera in the UAE, causing a fire that was later extinguished. While no group claimed responsibility, maritime security sources told Reuters at the time that the incident occurred outside the Strait of Hormuz and pointed to a widening of risks for commercial shipping. Earlier that week, a tanker was also struck off the coast of Qatar inside the Gulf. SPILL PUTTING COASTAL INFRASTRUCTURE AT RISK Maritime intelligence firm Windward first identified the spill on Tuesday, writing in a post on X that a VLCC-sized vessel was leaking oil about 25 km (16 miles) off Umm Al Quwain. Prevailing currents, it said at the time, could carry the slick southwest toward the UAE coastline. "Windward's drift model shows it reaching Sharjah's and Ajman's desalination intakes and ports by (October 22–23) if the leak isn't stopped," it wrote on X. Residents in some areas had posted on social media about strange odours. The ministry, however, said that odours reported in Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain posed no health risks. The smell was still pungent across Umm Al Quwain on Friday. The UAE relies on desalination plants for most of its drinking water, and much of the economy — including ports and industrial facilities — is also located on the coast, making any contamination along its shoreline particularly sensitive. The spill follows a separate tanker-related environmental incident in August, when oil from a tanker that ran aground off Oman began reaching the mainland coast. articles.title: Fatigue, fear and the flaws in shipping’s safety data
articles.summary: Seafarer fatigue, mental health and reluctance to report mistakes should become key considerations for marine insurers, banks and investors, according to new research warning that shipping is overlooking significant commercial risks hidden in its own data. The Sustainable Shipping Initiative’s (SSI) From Welfare to...
articles.body: Finance and Insurance Operations Fatigue, fear and the flaws in shipping’s safety data Sam Chambers October 23, 2026 0 202 1 minute read Britannia P&I Britannia P&I Seafarer fatigue, mental health and reluctance to report mistakes should become key considerations for marine insurers, banks and investors, according to new research warning that shipping is overlooking significant commercial risks hidden in its own data. The Sustainable Shipping Initiative’s (SSI) From Welfare to Risk report, published yesterday, examines 68 sources spanning accident investigations, insurance claims, academic studies and seafarer surveys. It finds consistent links between crew wellbeing and safety outcomes, particularly involving fatigue, mental health and psychological safety. Fatigue emerges as the most extensively documented risk factor. The report warns that understaffing and excessive workloads encourage the falsification of rest-hour records, concealing dangerous working conditions from compliance systems. Between a quarter and a third of seafarers do not feel safe raising concerns or reporting mistakes, potentially undermining the accuracy of incident and near-miss reporting. The findings reinforce earlier research covered by Splash . A World Maritime University study published in 2024 found 64.3% of surveyed seafarers adjusted their work/rest records. Another welfare review, reported by Splash last month, found just 49% of seafarers believed their most recent vessel carried sufficient crew to work safely without excessive fatigue. Insurance claims provide further evidence of the financial implications. Gard’s latest crew claims report identifies stress, fatigue and excessive workloads as important factors in onboard injuries, while illness accounts for almost 60% of crew claims. SSI argues insurers can already incorporate welfare indicators into loss-prevention programmes and underwriting discussions, while lenders could include them in borrower monitoring. However, the organisation cautions that current evidence remains insufficient to use welfare indicators as standalone predictors of future claims, insurance premiums or investment performance. The next challenge is connecting existing welfare surveys, accident investigations, port state control findings and insurance claims at vessel and operator level, allowing the industry to quantify how poor crew conditions translate into financial losses. Register On 28 September, APM Capital agreed to acquire a 53.35% stake in the parent of Euroports, an operator of more than 50 deep-sea and inland terminals across ten European countries and China that handles over 70 million tonnes of bulk, breakbulk and liquid bulk a year. On 20 October in Copenhagen, APM Terminals signed a memorandum of understanding with Vietnamese conglomerate Hateco for a rail freight terminal network in northern Vietnam valued at up to US$3.5 billion. They are two parallel tracks of a single strategy. APM Terminals, Maersk’s port unit, runs container terminals, and its investments follow the corridors that geopolitics is redrawing. Vietnam shows the template. APM began as an adviser to Hateco in 2023, took a 49% stake in the Haiphong international container terminal in April 2026, joined the Lien Chieu port project in Danang, and is now moving to the railhead. Each step pushes control further from the quay into the hinterland. The same logic runs through on-dock rail at Mobile, the rail-heavy Rijeka Gateway in Croatia, and Balboa in Panama, where APM took over operations in February after Panama’s Supreme Court annulled CK Hutchison’s concessions. APM Capital is a separate infrastructure fund manager backed by A.P. Moller Holding, and it invests where the container business does not reach. Euroports moves fertilizers, grain, sugar, metals and forest products, the commodities that keep European industry and food systems running. Coming after APMC’s investment in Spain’s BERGÉ Logistics, the deal gives the group a layered presence in Iberia: APM Terminals’ container gateways at Valencia and Barcelona, with bulk, breakbulk and logistics around them. APMC chief executive Kim Fejfer framed the purchase in the language of resilient supply chains and secure trade flows. Belgium’s public investors SFPIM and PMV remain Euroports shareholders, with SFPIM saying it intends to keep strategic assets anchored in Belgium. The Hateco agreement was signed during the state visit of Vietnam’s General Secretary and President Tô Lâm to Denmark. Balboa was handed over after the Panama Maritime Authority took possession of the port by decree. In each case the Maersk position is co-owned or endorsed by the government that hosts it. That is the reverse of the exposure that cost CK Hutchison its Panama ports. Panama Ports Company has brought arbitration in London against Maersk over Balboa, proceedings likely to take years. Euroports still needs regulatory approvals, expected in the first quarter of 2027, and its footprint includes terminals in China: a group building alternatives to Chinese port networks will hold assets under Chinese jurisdiction. Headline figures also run ahead of committed money. Hateco valued its earlier Haiphong port project with Maersk at US$400 million, roughly a ninth of the new rail ceiling, and Vietnam’s double-digit growth target is itself exposed to fuel disruption from the Iran war. Operating risk sits with APM Terminals, balance-sheet flexibility with A.P. Moller Capital, and political legitimacy is borrowed from host states. Where CMA CGM orchestrates its network with as few hard assets as possible, the APM Group layers them, across cargo types and transport modes, on corridors aligned with the West. Three markers will show whether the model holds: Panama’s long-term tender for Balboa, regulatory clearance for Euroports, and the first binding commitment under the Vietnam memorandum.

Together they form a single strategy of corridor control.

President Julius Maada Bio inaugurated Sierra Leone Ocean Shipping Company (SLOSCO) at Queen Elizabeth II Quay in Freetown earlier this week. The venture is 70% owned by Zhejiang Xiehai Group, with the remaining 30% held by the state-owned Sierra Leone National Shipping Agency (SLNSA). The company plans to establish a fleet of 50 ships, with an initial phase involving 30 vessels, targeting dry bulk, liquid bulk and other cargoes. Its principal markets include Sierra Leone’s substantial iron ore and bauxite exports, alongside imports of petroleum products, grain and other essential commodities. “For far too long, we have relied on international carriers to export and import our products,” Bio said. The new venture follows the restructuring of Sierra Leone’s longstanding national shipping company into SLNSA last year. Legislation provides the national carrier with rights covering 40% of the value of the country’s import and export cargoes. SLOSCO is headed by chief executive Sui Xiao, with former BRS Shipbrokers executive Laurent Debart serving as chief operating officer. The company has established operations in Freetown, Shanghai and Geneva. The venture represents another expansion of Chinese shipping interests in West Africa, with Freetown seeking to retain more of the freight revenue generated by its international trade. Canada’s Hampton Financial, which holds 325,000 Icon shares representing approximately 9% of the company, has disclosed a letter sent to Icon’s management demanding changes to its preferred shares, dividend arrangements and corporate governance. It also wants a one-for-one share dividend for existing ordinary shareholders and the appointment of a Hampton-nominated director. The investor argues that these measures would address dilution concerns while preserving Panagiotidi’s control of the business. The proposals have not been accepted or implemented, and the filing does not establish that legal proceedings have commenced. Icon, established in 2023, operates three bulk carriers.
